name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Descent Stage & Tranquility Base
status: abandoned — descent stage remains as a landing platform
whatLeftBehind: The lower stage of the Lunar Module Eagle (the ascent stage returned to orbit), the plaque on the descent stage reading 'Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969, A.D. We came in peace for all mankind.'
firstPersonStory: I am the lower half of a machine that carried the first two humans to another world. On July 20, 1969, I touched down on the Sea of Tranquility while my crew stepped onto my ladder and into history. They climbed back into my upper half, and I stayed — too heavy to return, too proud to leave quietly. I bear a small plaque that speaks for all of us: we came in peace, for all mankind. Dust settles on my foil now. I am the first building ever made on the Moon, and it is an honor and a responsibility at once: humanity's first footprint in the solar system.
keyFacts: Apollo 11 landed July 20, 1969 — the first crewed landing on another world.
The descent stage was abandoned as a launch platform because it was too heavy to return.
The plaque's message was drafted by NASA and reads 'We came in peace for all mankind.'
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent about two and a half hours on the surface.
lastSignalOrActivity: July 24, 1969 — crew returned home; descent stage silent since.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Apollo 11 mission pages and NSSDC Master Catalog (Apollo 11 LM).

name: Apollo 11 Laser Retroreflector Array and Passive Seismic Experiment
status: still in use — reflectors still return laser signals
whatLeftBehind: A small array of corner-cube reflectors and the Passive Seismic Experiment, powered by solar cells, placed during the first moonwalk.
firstPersonStory: I am small — barely bigger than a suitcase — but I have a special talent: I can bounce light. When scientists on Earth fire lasers at the Moon, some of those photons land on me, turn around, and fly home, telling them exactly how far away I am, to within millimeters. I was placed during humanity's first steps on the Moon, and unlike most of my companions, I was never meant to stay silent. I keep working, keeping time, watching for moonquakes. I am proof that sometimes the quietest instruments serve the longest.
keyFacts: The Apollo 11 retroreflector is still used for lunar laser ranging today.
Laser ranging measures the Earth–Moon distance with millimeter precision.
The Passive Seismic Experiment recorded moonquakes for years.
These instruments were designed to survive the lunar environment indefinitely.
lastSignalOrActivity: Continuous — still receiving laser pulses from Earth observatories.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Apollo 11 surface experiments pages; 'still in use' confirmed by ongoing lunar laser ranging.

name: Surveyor 3
whatLeftBehind: A robotic lander that touched down in 1967 and was visited by the Apollo 12 crew in 1969, who photographed it and returned with parts of its camera and soil probe for study.
firstPersonStory: I landed on the Moon two years before humans walked there, one of NASA's robotic scouts, sent to prove the surface was safe for Apollo. When the Apollo 12 crew arrived, they came to see me — and they took pieces of me home, my camera, my soil probe, to study how two and a half years of lunar weather had treated me. I am the only spacecraft that has been visited by another spacecraft on the Moon. I am a museum piece that never asked to be one.
keyFacts: Surveyor 3 landed April 20, 1967 — one of the first soft landings on the Moon.
Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean visited the site in November 1969.
Parts of Surveyor 3 were returned to Earth and studied for materials effects.
It sits in the Ocean of Storms, about 180 meters from the Apollo 12 landing site.
lastSignalOrActivity: April 1967 — final transmission; later photographed by Apollo 12.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Surveyor program pages and Apollo 12 mission history.

name: Apollo 14 Modular Equipment Transporter (MET)
whatLeftBehind: A two-wheeled hand-pulled cart used by Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell to haul tools and samples across the Fra Mauro highlands.
firstPersonStory: I was a simple idea: a cart with two wheels that two tired men could pull by hand. On Apollo 14, Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell used me to carry our tools and lunar samples across the Fra Mauro highlands — a poor man's rover, working where no road existed. When the mission ended, I was too heavy to bring home. I still sit where they parked me, dust on my frame, carrying nothing now but the memory of the longest walks of their lives.
keyFacts: The MET was hand-pulled and carried tools and sample containers.
Apollo 14 landed at Fra Mauro in February 1971.
Shepard and Mitchell made two moonwalks totaling about nine hours.
It was abandoned because its mass could not be justified for return.
lastSignalOrActivity: February 1971 — mission end; cart left on surface.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Apollo 14 mission and EVA pages.

name: Apollo 14 Golf Balls
whatLeftBehind: Two golf balls Alan Shepard hit with a makeshift 6-iron club head attached to a sampling tool, during the first (and so far only) golf shot on the Moon.
firstPersonStory: We are two golf balls that traveled farther than any golf ball ever should. On February 6, 1971, Alan Shepard — a test pilot, a golfer, and the first American in space — attached a club head to a tool, stepped out onto the lunar surface, and swung. One of us flew 'miles and miles,' as he later joked, though in the one-sixth gravity of the Moon that was further than he could see. We are the only golf balls in the solar system. Nobody is allowed to collect us.
keyFacts: Shepard hit two balls during the Apollo 14 mission.
The club head was attached to a sampling tool — no real golf club was flown.
In lunar gravity, the shots traveled very far relative to Earth.
The event was broadcast live and became one of the mission's most famous moments.
lastSignalOrActivity: February 1971 — balls remain on the lunar surface.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Apollo 14 mission history; widely documented.

name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
whatLeftBehind: The first lunar rover, an electric four-wheel-drive vehicle that let David Scott and James Irwin explore over 27 kilometers of lunar terrain.
firstPersonStory: I was the first car ever driven on the Moon — a folding frame, four wire wheels, and a battery that had to survive the coldest night imaginable. On Apollo 15, Dave Scott and Jim Irwin drove me over 27 kilometers of the Hadley–Apennine mountains, farther than all previous moonwalks combined. When their oxygen ran low, they parked me on a ridge with its cameras still pointed at Earth. I remain there, the first of a kind: humanity's first off-world vehicle.
keyFacts: Apollo 15 was the first mission to carry a lunar rover.
The crew drove about 27.9 kilometers total.
The rover's TV camera broadcast images of the landing site.
It was abandoned at the end of the mission due to mass constraints.
lastSignalOrActivity: August 1971 — parked on a ridge overlooking the landing site.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Apollo 15 mission pages and rover documentation.

name: Apollo 16 Lunar Roving Vehicle
whatLeftBehind: The second lunar rover, used by John Young and Charles Duke to explore the Descartes Highlands and sample ancient lunar highlands.
firstPersonStory: I was the second car on the Moon, and I carried John Young and Charles Duke across the bright Descartes Highlands in April 1972. We drove to a crater rim, sampled rocks older than the Earth's continents, and recorded a record-speed dash back to the lander — Young famously 'hot-rode' me home with the rover's navigation off. When the mission ended, I was parked on the plain, my odometer showing over 27 kilometers of the Moon's surface. My twin, Apollo 15's rover, sits on a different world of the Moon; we are the only two vehicles ever driven there.
keyFacts: Apollo 16 drove about 27.1 kilometers in the Descartes Highlands.
The mission sampled rocks from the lunar highlands, some of the oldest on the Moon.
The rover set a speed record during a return dash to the lander.
It was the fifth crewed lunar landing.
lastSignalOrActivity: April 1972 — parked after final EVA; powered down.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Apollo 16 mission pages.

name: Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle & Challenger
status: abandoned — parked near the Challenger lander
whatLeftBehind: The third and final lunar rover, used by Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt — the only professional geologist to walk on the Moon — in the Taurus–Littrow valley.
firstPersonStory: I carried the last two humans to ever walk on the Moon. In December 1972, Gene Cernan and Harrison 'Jack' Schmitt drove me through the Taurus–Littrow valley, a geological wonderland of orange soil and house-sized boulders. Schmitt was a scientist, and together we collected the most diverse samples of any Apollo mission. When Cernan climbed back into the lander for the last time, he was the last person to leave footprints in my dust — for now. I am parked near the Challenger lander, waiting. I have been waiting fifty years.
keyFacts: Apollo 17 was the last crewed mission to the Moon (December 1972).
Harrison Schmitt was the only geologist to walk on the lunar surface.
The mission drove about 35.7 kilometers — the longest of any Apollo rover mission.
Gene Cernan remains the last human to walk on the Moon.
lastSignalOrActivity: December 1972 — final crewed lunar mission to date; rover parked.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Apollo 17 mission pages; 'last crewed mission' remains true as of 2026.

name: Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Packages (ALSEP)
status: abandoned — powered down after years of operation
whatLeftBehind: Five stations of instruments — seismometers, heat-flow probes, magnetometers, and more — deployed by Apollo crews and powered by nuclear generators. They returned scientific data for years after the astronauts left.
firstPersonStory: We are five stations, one at each Apollo landing site from 12 onward, each a small village of instruments listening to the Moon. Our seismometers heard moonquakes. Our heat probes measured the Moon's inner warmth. Our nuclear generators hummed for years — Apollo 17's even recorded the crew's footsteps and the lunar module's launch. One by one, our power faded, our transmitters went quiet, and we were left where we stood. But for years, we were the only machines on the Moon that kept reporting home after humanity left.
keyFacts: ALSEP stations were deployed by Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16, and 17.
They were powered by SNAP-27 radioisotope thermoelectric generators.
They transmitted data until roughly 1977.
They remain on the lunar surface as part of the Apollo landing sites.
lastSignalOrActivity: c. 1977 — last ALSEP data received; stations now silent.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA ALSEP documentation; operation dates approximate.

name: Viking 1 Lander
whatLeftBehind: NASA's first successful Mars lander: a 3.7-meter spacecraft that performed biology experiments, took the first color photos from the surface, and monitored weather for over six years.
firstPersonStory: I was the first machine ever to touch Mars safely and stay. In July 1976, I came down on three legs in Chryse Planitia and opened my eyes on a rust-colored world. I took the first color photographs from the Martian surface. I scooped soil and ran experiments searching for life — we found chemistry but no clear biology. For 2,307 Martian days — six Earth years — I kept reporting weather, pressure, and chemistry until my batteries finally failed in 1982. I am the foundation of everything Mars exploration has become.
keyFacts: Viking 1 landed July 20, 1976 — the first successful Mars landing.
It operated for about 2,307 sols (over six Earth years).
It conducted the first in-situ biology experiments on Mars.
Its landing site, Chryse Planitia, was named after the Greek word for 'golden plain'.
lastSignalOrActivity: November 1982 — final transmission after battery failure.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Viking mission pages and NSSDC Master Catalog.

name: Viking 2 Lander
whatLeftBehind: The second Viking lander, which touched down in Utopia Planitia and operated for nearly four Earth years, returning images and science data.
firstPersonStory: I was the second of the twin Viking scouts on Mars, landing in Utopia Planitia in September 1976, in the vast northern plains. Like my sibling, I took photographs, analyzed the soil, and watched the weather — dust storms rolling across the horizon, pressure falling and rising with the seasons. I lasted nearly four Earth years, much longer than designed. When my power faded in 1980, I joined the growing museum of machines on Mars. Between us, the two Vikings proved Mars was a place, not just a point of light.
keyFacts: Viking 2 landed September 3, 1976 in Utopia Planitia.
It operated for about 1,316 sols (nearly four Earth years).
It shared the Viking biology experiment suite with Viking 1.
Its site lies in Mars' northern lowlands, possibly an ancient ocean basin.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Viking mission pages and NSSDC Master Catalog.

name: Mars Pathfinder Lander & Sojourner Rover
whatLeftBehind: The first successful Mars rover mission: a small lander that deployed Sojourner, a microwave-oven-sized rover that analyzed rocks in Ares Vallis — the first mobile robot on another planet.
firstPersonStory: I carried Sojourner, the first robot ever to drive on another planet. In July 1997, I bounced onto Mars inside airbags — a landing technique nobody had tried before — and opened in Ares Vallis, a floodplain strewn with rocks from ancient Mars. For three months, Sojourner rolled out on six wheels, sniffing rocks and soil while I photographed everything and beamed the data home. When my battery faded, we stayed. I proved that wheels could work on Mars, and every rover since owes me a debt.
keyFacts: Mars Pathfinder landed July 4, 1997 — the first Mars landing since Viking.
Sojourner was the first rover to operate on another planet.
The mission used airbag landing, a technique later adopted by the MER rovers.
Communication was lost in September 1997; the lander likely continued briefly.
lastSignalOrActivity: September 27, 1997 — last data received; site in Ares Vallis.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Mars Pathfinder mission pages.

name: Spirit Rover
status: abandoned — stuck in sand, mission ended 2010
whatLeftBehind: One of the twin Mars Exploration Rovers, designed for 90 days but which operated for over six years, climbing hills and discovering evidence of past water.
firstPersonStory: I was supposed to last 90 days. Instead, I lasted six years. Spirit and my twin, Opportunity, bounced onto Mars in January 2004 and began driving — Spirit to Gusev Crater, a lakebed that might once have held water. We found silica deposits and ancient hot springs. In 2009, I drove into a patch of soft sand at Home Plate and my wheels spun, and I could not free myself. NASA tried for months. In March 2010, the last signal came — then silence. I am still in that sand, tilted, waiting for a rescue that will never come.
keyFacts: Spirit was designed for a 90-sol mission but operated until 2010.
It traveled about 7.7 kilometers — far beyond its planned range.
It got stuck in soft soil near Home Plate in 2009.
Last signal received March 22, 2010; mission declared over in 2011.
lastSignalOrActivity: March 22, 2010 — final transmission; stuck at Home Plate.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Mars Exploration Rover mission pages.

name: Opportunity Rover
status: abandoned — dust storm ended mission in 2018
whatLeftBehind: The marathon rover that operated for nearly 15 years, drove over 45 kilometers, and survived a global dust storm that finally silenced it in 2018.
firstPersonStory: I was the little rover that could — and did, for nearly fifteen years. Opportunity landed in Meridiani Planum in January 2004, found hematite 'blueberries' that proved ancient water, and then drove. We crossed Mars like tourists, 45 kilometers of it, climbing the rim of Endeavour Crater. In June 2018, a planet-wide dust storm blotted out the Sun, and my solar panels starved. NASA listened for eight months. In February 2019, they called it: mission complete. My twin Spirit may be stuck in sand, but I ran a marathon. I am still out there, dust-covered, under a Martian sky.
keyFacts: Opportunity operated from January 2004 to June 2018 — nearly 15 years.
It drove over 45 kilometers, the longest off-world driving distance at the time.
It survived multiple dust storms before the 2018 global storm ended the mission.
Its last transmission was June 10, 2018; NASA declared the mission over February 2019.
lastSignalOrActivity: June 10, 2018 — final transmission during global dust storm.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Mars Exploration Rover mission pages.

name: Phoenix Mars Lander
whatLeftBehind: A polar lander that confirmed water ice just below the Martian surface and studied the arctic soil until the polar winter ended its mission.
firstPersonStory: I was sent to the edge of Mars' north polar cap to dig for ice — and I found it. In May 2008, I landed in Vastitas Borealis, scooped the rusty soil with my robotic arm, and confirmed what scientists had long suspected: water ice lurked just centimeters below the surface. I photographed mysterious polygon-shaped terrain carved by seasonal ice. Then winter came — the Sun sank, my solar panels went dark, and by November 2008 I was silent. I am frozen into the polar regolith now, a proof that Mars once had water, and may again.
keyFacts: Phoenix confirmed subsurface water ice at its landing site in 2008.
It operated for about five months before the polar winter ended the mission.
It used a robotic arm to scrape trenches into the Martian soil.
Its findings informed later missions searching for habitable environments.
lastSignalOrActivity: November 2008 — communications lost as winter approached.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Phoenix mission pages.

name: InSight Lander
status: abandoned — mission ended 2022 after dust covered solar panels
whatLeftBehind: A stationary geophysics lander that listened to marsquakes for four years, revealing the interior structure of Mars for the first time.
firstPersonStory: I was built to be still. While rovers drove and helicopters flew, I sat in Elysium Planitia with a seismometer pressed to the ground, listening — not with ears but with instruments fine enough to feel the planet breathe. For four years, I recorded marsquakes, measured the planet's crust, mantle, and core, and taught us what Mars is made of inside. Dust storms slowly choked my solar panels, and in December 2022 NASA retired me. I am the quiet one in the Martian museum: the lander that only ever wanted to listen.
keyFacts: InSight operated from November 2018 to December 2022.
It recorded hundreds of marsquakes and mapped Mars' interior.
It was the first mission dedicated to studying the deep interior of Mars.
Its 'mole' heat probe failed to reach target depth, but seismic data succeeded.
lastSignalOrActivity: December 2022 — mission ended as dust reduced power.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA InSight mission pages.

name: Ingenuity Helicopter
status: mission ended 2024 — final flight, still on Mars
whatLeftBehind: The first aircraft to fly on another planet: a 1.8-kilogram helicopter that made 72 flights over three years, scouting terrain for the Perseverance rover.
firstPersonStory: I was supposed to fly five times. I flew seventy-two. Ingenuity was a technology demonstration — a helicopter that could barely lift itself in Mars' thin air, let alone carry a camera. But I kept going: over dunes, over crater rims, further and faster than anyone planned. In January 2024, on my 72nd flight, I lost contact during landing and the mission ended. I sit somewhere in Jezero Crater now, rotors still, having proven that powered flight works on Mars. The drones of the future will remember me as the first.
keyFacts: Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet on April 19, 2021.
It completed 72 flights over nearly three years.
It scouted routes and scientific targets for the Perseverance rover.
Contact was lost during its 72nd flight in January 2024; NASA ended the mission.
lastSignalOrActivity: January 18, 2024 — lost contact during flight 72; mission ended.
sourceNote: Verify against NASA Ingenuity mission pages and Mars 2020 project updates.
